title: Climate Justice: CBDR, Loss and Damage, Stocktake

cards.b:
Almost every climate negotiation is a fight over fairness: who caused the problem, who pays and who adapts. Prelims asks about CBDR, Annexes and funds. Mains asks you to argue India's case.

The key terms are CBDR-RC, climate finance, the Loss and Damage Fund and the Global Stocktake.

CBDR comes from Principle 7 of the Rio Declaration (1992) and Article 3 of the UNFCCC. All states share a common duty to protect the climate, but their duties differ because they contributed differently and have different capacity. The Kyoto Protocol (1997) divided states into Annex I (developed countries, with binding targets) and non-Annex I. The Paris Agreement (2015) moved to nationally determined contributions (NDCs) from all, and added "in the light of different national circumstances" (CBDR-RC).

India and China insist on keeping the differentiation.

At Copenhagen (2009), developed countries promised US$100 billion a year by 2020. It was reached late, and the OECD said it was met in 2022. The Green Climate Fund (set up at Cancun 2010; HQ Songdo, South Korea) is the main fund. The Adaptation Fund and GEF also work.

At COP29 (Baku, 2024), a New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) set US$300 billion a year by 2035 from developed countries, within a wider aim of US$1.3 trillion from all sources. India called the figure too low.

Loss and damage means harm from climate change that adaptation cannot avoid, like island loss or flood damage. The Warsaw International Mechanism (2013) began the work. At COP27 (Sharm el-Sheikh, 2022), countries agreed to set up a fund. At COP28 (Dubai, 2023) it was made operational on day one, with initial pledges of about US$700 million. The World Bank hosts it as an interim step.

The Santiago Network gives technical help. Small island states and the least developed countries pushed for this for decades.

Article 14 of the Paris Agreement requires a Global Stocktake (GST) every five years to measure collective progress. The first GST ended at COP28 (2023) with a call to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems, the first time such wording entered a COP decision. It also called for tripling renewable energy capacity and doubling energy efficiency by 2030. Countries will submit new NDCs by 2025 informed by it.

COP26 (Glasgow 2021) had agreed to phase down unabated coal, a wording India and China changed from "phase out".

India says rich countries used up much of the carbon budget. India's per-capita emissions are about 2 tonnes of CO2, far below the US and EU (figures vary by year). It argues for climate equity, technology transfer and finance, and opposes unilateral trade measures like the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which taxes carbon in imports from 2026.

India also pushes LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment, 2021) as a demand-side idea.

cards.h: Who is a developing country now?
cards.b: The Annex lists of 1992 are old. China is the largest emitter today, and Gulf states are rich. Developed countries say big emitters must pay. Poorer states say historical responsibility remains. The BASIC group (Brazil, South Africa, India, China) and the Like-Minded Developing Countries hold the line on differentiation, while the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS) wants faster cuts.

India submitted its updated NDC in August 2022 (45 percent cut in emissions intensity from 2005 levels and 50 percent non-fossil power capacity by 2030) and announced Panchamrit at COP26. At COP28 India did not sign the pledge to triple renewable capacity, citing the need to treat all energy sources and equity fairly.

• CBDR: Rio 1992, Principle 7.
  • $100 bn: Copenhagen 2009.
  • GCF: Cancun 2010, Songdo.
  • Loss and Damage Fund: agreed COP27 2022; operational COP28 2023.
  • GST: Article 14; first at COP28.
  • NCQG: COP29, $300 bn by 2035.

Also hold: COP26 Glasgow 2021 for Panchamrit and coal phase down; COP28 Dubai 2023 for the stocktake.

Prelims-style: "CBDR principle was first recognised in" (Rio Declaration 1992). "The Green Climate Fund is headquartered in" (Songdo).

Mains-style: "Explain climate justice and India's stand on climate finance." Structure: history and CBDR; finance gaps; loss and damage; GST; India's per-capita and historical argument; CBAM; way forward.
